```{r, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R", local = TRUE)
```

A proportional-odds model assumes that each covariate shifts the odds of
being in a worse state by the same factor at every cut-point of the ordinal
scale. For example, the effect of time on the odds of being in hospital or
worse is assumed to equal its effect on the odds of death. When this
assumption is doubtful for some covariates, a *partial* proportional-odds
model lets their effects differ between cut-points while keeping proportional
odds for the others.

This article fits both kinds of model to the same data with `vglm_markov()`:
a full proportional-odds model, and a partial proportional-odds model in which
the effect of time differs between the cut-points. We compare how well the
two models fit, and how closely each reproduces the observed state occupancy
probabilities (SOPs), transitions, and correlations between days.

## Simulate data

We simulate 1,000 patients over 28 days with `sim_markov("violet")`. Its
trajectories resemble those of the
[VIOLET trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1911124) of vitamin D3 in
critically ill adults, and each patient's starting state, age, and SOFA
(Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score are drawn from the VIOLET
patients. There are four states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 | At home |
| 2 | In hospital or another health care facility |
| 3 | On a ventilator or with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) |
| 4 | Dead |

Death is absorbing. Treated patients (`tx = 1`) have 0.8 times the odds of
being in a worse state on any day.

The simulator itself is a partial proportional-odds model, described in
`?violet_preset`. Time enters as a straight line whose slope changes after
day 2, and both slopes differ between the three cut-points. During the first
two days, each day lowers the log odds of being in hospital or worse by 1.315,
so many patients go home, but raises the log odds of death by 0.412. After
day 2 all three slopes are close to zero. A single time effect shared by all
cut-points cannot describe both trends, so we can check which model recovers
this structure.

```{r setup}
library(mostr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(rms)
library(VGAM)

N_PATIENTS <- 1000
FOLLOW_UP <- 28
SEED <- 20261009
STATE_LEVELS <- as.character(1:4)
ABSORB <- "4"

raw_data <- sim_markov(
  "violet",
  n_patients = N_PATIENTS,
  follow_up_time = FOLLOW_UP,
  treatment_effect = log(0.8),
  seed = SEED
)

model_data <- prepare_markov_data(raw_data, absorbing_state = 4)
```

## Fit the proportional-odds model

Both models use treatment, the previous state, age, SOFA score, and the same
time trend as the simulator: `time` and `pmax(time - 2, 0)`, the number of
days after day 2. Together they form a straight line whose slope changes
after day 2.

In VGAM, `cumulative(reverse = TRUE)` models the odds of worse (higher)
states, and `parallel = TRUE` requests proportional odds for every term.

```{r fit-po}
form <- ordered(y) ~ tx + time + pmax(time - 2, 0) + yprev + age + sofa

fit_po <- vglm_markov(
  form,
  family = VGAM::cumulative(reverse = TRUE, parallel = TRUE),
  data = model_data,
  id_var = "id"
)
```

## Specify which effects may vary

VGAM expresses partial proportional odds through *constraint matrices*. The
model has one linear predictor per cut-point; with four states there are
three, for "state 2 or worse", "state 3 or worse", and "state 4" (dead). Each
model term has a constraint matrix with one row per cut-point and one column
per coefficient for that term:

- a single column of ones gives one coefficient shared by all cut-points,
  which is proportional odds;
- an identity matrix, with one column per cut-point, gives the term a
  separate coefficient at every cut-point.

The easiest way to obtain a valid set of constraint matrices is to fit the
proportional-odds model first and edit its constraints. We change two things:

1. The two time terms get identity matrices, so that each cut-point has its
   own time slopes, as in the simulator.
2. The fitted model lists a separate constraint for each dummy variable of the
   factor `yprev`. The constraints we supply must instead be named by the
   formula term, so we replace these entries with a single `yprev` entry with
   proportional odds.

```{r constraints}
constraints <- fit_po$vglm_fit@constraints

# One row per cut-point: three for four states.
n_thresholds <- nrow(constraints[["time"]])

# Replace the per-dummy yprev constraints with one term-level entry.
yprev_terms <- grep("^yprev", names(constraints), value = TRUE)
constraints[yprev_terms] <- NULL
constraints[["yprev"]] <- cbind(PO_effect = rep(1, n_thresholds))

# A separate time slope at each cut-point.
time_terms <- c("time", "pmax(time - 2, 0)")
constraints[time_terms] <- list(diag(n_thresholds))
constraints[["time"]]
```

## Fit the partial proportional-odds model

We refit the model with these constraints. `parallel = FALSE` tells VGAM not
to impose proportional odds on every term, so that our constraint matrices
decide instead. Starting from the proportional-odds fit's linear predictors
(`etastart`) helps the fit converge. The final line stores the constraint
list itself, rather than the name `constraints`, in the model call, so that
code that later re-evaluates the call does not depend on this variable.

```{r fit-ppo}
fit_ppo <- vglm_markov(
  form,
  family = VGAM::cumulative(reverse = TRUE, parallel = FALSE),
  data = model_data,
  id_var = "id",
  constraints = constraints,
  etastart = fit_po$vglm_fit@predictors
)
fit_ppo$vglm_fit@call$constraints <- constraints
```

VGAM numbers the coefficients of a term by the columns of its constraint
matrix, so the time slopes of the partial proportional-odds model end in `:1`
for "state 2 or worse", `:2` for "state 3 or worse", and `:3` for death. The
proportional-odds model has one slope for each time term. We compare both
with the slopes used by the simulator:

```{r compare-coefficients}
coef_po <- coef(fit_po$vglm_fit)
coef_ppo <- coef(fit_ppo$vglm_fit)

data.frame(
  term = rep(time_terms, each = n_thresholds),
  cutoff = rep(c("hospital or worse", "ventilator/ARDS or dead", "dead"), 2),
  PO = rep(coef_po[time_terms], each = n_thresholds),
  PPO = coef_ppo[paste0(rep(time_terms, each = n_thresholds), ":", 1:3)],
  simulated = c(-1.315, -0.481, 0.412, 1.384, 0.525, -0.410),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

The partial proportional-odds slopes are close to the simulated ones, while
the proportional-odds model replaces them with one compromise slope for each
time term. Both models estimate the treatment effect well; the simulated
value is $\log(0.8) \approx -0.22$:

```{r compare-treatment}
c(PO = coef_po[["tx"]], PPO = coef_ppo[["tx"]], simulated = log(0.8))
```

## Compare model fit

The Akaike information criterion, `AIC()`, measures how well a model fits
the data while penalizing each extra coefficient by 2 units; lower values are
better. The Bayesian information criterion, `BIC()`, penalizes each
coefficient by the logarithm of the number of observations instead. A
difference of more than about 10 is usually regarded as strong evidence for
the model with the lower value. Because the proportional-odds model is the
partial proportional-odds model with the time slopes forced to be equal, we
can also compare them with a likelihood ratio test, `VGAM::lrtest()`.

```{r model-fit}
data.frame(
  model = c("Proportional odds", "Partial proportional odds"),
  coefficients = c(length(coef_po), length(coef_ppo)),
  AIC = c(AIC(fit_po$vglm_fit), AIC(fit_ppo$vglm_fit)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit_po$vglm_fit), BIC(fit_ppo$vglm_fit))
)

VGAM::lrtest(fit_ppo$vglm_fit, fit_po$vglm_fit)
```

AIC and the likelihood ratio test strongly favour the partial
proportional-odds model. BIC is about the same for both models: with about
25,500 daily observations it charges about 10 units for each of the four
extra coefficients, which nearly cancels their improvement in fit.

## Compare state occupancy probabilities

`avg_sops()` estimates, for each arm, the probability of each state on each
day, averaged over the patients' observed starting states and covariates (see
`vignette("full-po-sops")`). We compare both models' estimates with the
observed proportion of patients in each state, separately for each arm. Only
point estimates are needed here, so we do not call `inferences()`.

```{r sops-models}
sop_args <- list(
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = seq_len(FOLLOW_UP),
  y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
  absorb = ABSORB
)
sop_po <- do.call(avg_sops, c(list(fit_po), sop_args))
sop_ppo <- do.call(avg_sops, c(list(fit_ppo), sop_args))

observed <- as.data.frame(
  prop.table(
    table(
      tx = raw_data$tx,
      time = raw_data$time,
      state = factor(raw_data$y, levels = STATE_LEVELS)
    ),
    margin = c(1, 2)
  ),
  responseName = "estimate"
)

sop_comparison <- rbind(
  data.frame(source = "Observed", observed[, c("tx", "time", "state", "estimate")]),
  data.frame(source = "Proportional odds", as.data.frame(sop_po)[, c("tx", "time", "state", "estimate")]),
  data.frame(source = "Partial proportional odds", as.data.frame(sop_ppo)[, c("tx", "time", "state", "estimate")])
)
sop_comparison$time <- as.integer(as.character(sop_comparison$time))
sop_comparison$source <- factor(
  sop_comparison$source,
  levels = c("Observed", "Proportional odds", "Partial proportional odds")
)
```

```{r sops-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(
  subset(sop_comparison, tx == 0),
  aes(time, estimate, colour = source, linetype = source)
) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~state, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Day",
    y = "State occupancy probability",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    title = "Control arm"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Both models follow the observed proportions closely, but the
proportional-odds model makes two systematic errors. It sends patients home
too slowly in the second week, leaving about 3 percentage points too many in
hospital, and it puts too many deaths on day 1 and too few during the second
and third weeks. The mean absolute difference from the observed proportions
over all days, states, and arms summarizes this:

```{r sops-error}
sop_wide <- reshape(
  sop_comparison,
  idvar = c("tx", "time", "state"),
  timevar = "source",
  direction = "wide"
)
c(
  `Proportional odds` = mean(abs(
    sop_wide$`estimate.Proportional odds` - sop_wide$estimate.Observed
  )),
  `Partial proportional odds` = mean(abs(
    sop_wide$`estimate.Partial proportional odds` - sop_wide$estimate.Observed
  ))
)
```

## Compare transitions

`plot_transitions()` shows, for selected days, the proportion of all
patients who move from each previous state (x-axis) to each current state
(y-axis). For the observed data these are counts divided by the number of
patients; for a model they are the expected proportions implied by its
transition probabilities.

```{r transitions-data}
transition_sources <- list(
  Observed = plot_transitions(
    raw_data,
    times = seq_len(FOLLOW_UP),
    y_levels = STATE_LEVELS
  ),
  `Proportional odds` = plot_transitions(
    fit_po,
    times = seq_len(FOLLOW_UP),
    y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
    absorb = ABSORB
  ),
  `Partial proportional odds` = plot_transitions(
    fit_ppo,
    times = seq_len(FOLLOW_UP),
    y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
    absorb = ABSORB
  )
)
transitions <- do.call(rbind, Map(
  function(plot, source) {
    data.frame(
      source = source,
      time = as.integer(as.character(plot$data$.time_key)),
      previous_state = plot$data$previous_state,
      state = plot$data$state,
      estimate = plot$data$estimate
    )
  },
  transition_sources,
  names(transition_sources)
))
transitions$source <- factor(transitions$source, levels = names(transition_sources))
```

```{r transitions-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(
  subset(transitions, time %in% c(2, 7, 14, 28)),
  aes(previous_state, state, fill = estimate)
) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  facet_grid(source ~ time, labeller = labeller(time = function(x) paste("Day", x))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "sqrt", limits = c(0, NA)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Previous state", y = "Current state", fill = "Proportion")
```

Most patients stay in their previous state, so the diagonal dominates all
three rows. Differences between the models appear in the smaller
off-diagonal proportions. The plotted values are easier to compare directly
over time. For example, the proportion of patients who die on each day after
being on a ventilator or with ARDS the day before:

```{r transitions-death, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(
  subset(transitions, previous_state == "3" & state == "4"),
  aes(time, estimate, colour = source, linetype = source)
) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Day",
    y = "Proportion of patients",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    title = "Moves from ventilator or ARDS (state 3) to death (state 4)"
  )
```

The proportional-odds model, which must give death the same time trend as
leaving hospital, overestimates these deaths on day 1 and underestimates
them during the following week. The partial proportional-odds model follows
the observed proportions.

## Compare correlations between days

`plot_correlation()` shows the Spearman rank correlation between patients'
states on every pair of days, from the observed data or implied by a model.

```{r correlation, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
correlation_days <- seq(1, FOLLOW_UP, by = 3)

correlation_plots <- list(
  plot_correlation(
    raw_data,
    times = correlation_days,
    fill_limits = c(0, 1),
    show_values = FALSE
  ) +
    labs(title = "Observed"),
  plot_correlation(
    fit_po,
    times = correlation_days,
    y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
    absorb = ABSORB,
    fill_limits = c(0, 1),
    show_values = FALSE
  ) +
    labs(title = "Proportional odds"),
  plot_correlation(
    fit_ppo,
    times = correlation_days,
    y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
    absorb = ABSORB,
    fill_limits = c(0, 1),
    show_values = FALSE
  ) +
    labs(title = "Partial proportional odds")
)
wrap_plots(correlation_plots, nrow = 1) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

All three plots look almost the same. Correlations between days depend
mainly on how strongly patients tend to stay in their previous state, which both models capture.

## Compare treatment effects on time in each state

`avg_comparisons()` with `estimand = "time_in_state"` sums each arm's daily
SOPs over follow-up. The result is the expected number of days spent in each
state, and the comparison reports treated minus control. A positive
difference for state 1 means that treated patients are expected to spend more
of the 28 days at home.

Analytical confidence intervals (`method = "delta"`) are available only for
full proportional-odds models, so for the partial proportional-odds model we
use `method = "mvn"`. It draws coefficient vectors from a multivariate normal
distribution centered on the estimates, with the model's covariance matrix,
recomputes the result for each draw, and takes percentiles. We use only 100
draws to keep this example fast; use more, such as 1,000, in a real analysis.

```{r time-in-state}
tis_args <- list(
  estimand = "time_in_state",
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = seq_len(FOLLOW_UP),
  y_levels = STATE_LEVELS,
  absorb = ABSORB
)

tis_po <- do.call(avg_comparisons, c(list(fit_po), tis_args)) |>
  inferences(method = "delta", vcov = "conditional")
tis_ppo <- do.call(avg_comparisons, c(list(fit_ppo), tis_args)) |>
  inferences(method = "mvn", n_draws = 100, seed = SEED)

tis_comparison <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = "Proportional odds", as.data.frame(tis_po)),
  data.frame(model = "Partial proportional odds", as.data.frame(tis_ppo))
)
tis_comparison$model <- factor(
  tis_comparison$model,
  levels = c("Proportional odds", "Partial proportional odds")
)
tis_comparison[, c("model", "state_set", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

```{r time-in-state-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(
  tis_comparison,
  aes(state_set, estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, colour = model)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(
    x = "State",
    y = "Difference in days (treated - control)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The two models give similar treatment effects even though their SOPs differ.
